claim: The paper reports that an sEMG-driven adaptive joint-impedance controller improved the tested open-space human–robot collaborative task relative to fixed low- and high-impedance modes: the variable-impedance mode had the shortest mean completion time, lowest mean interaction force, and lowest trajectory error. These findings are limited to the reported fixed-trajectory experiments and do not establish formal closed-loop stability, universal safety, or cross-user generalization.
claim_locator: Abstract; controller-method sections on intention estimation and adaptive impedance; experimental-results section and mode-comparison figures/tables; conclusion
epistemic_status: primary experimental robotics study with author-reported comparative results; theoretical and external-validity claims remain bounded
problem_and_setting: Human–robot collaboration in nominally open-space manipulation, where the robot should respond compliantly to human motion intent while retaining sufficient impedance for accurate trajectory tracking. The evaluation compares adaptive variable impedance against fixed low- and high-impedance control during collaborative dragging/tracking along a prescribed trajectory.
method_or_mechanism: The controller estimates the human collaborator's motion intention from surface electromyography signals and uses that estimate to adapt robot joint impedance online. The intended mechanism is to reduce resistance during rapid or freely guided motion and increase impedance when accurate tracking is required, thereby trading off interaction effort, completion speed, and tracking precision.
content_summary: The study presents an intention-driven adaptive impedance strategy for open-space human–robot collaboration. Surface electromyography is used as an input for estimating human intention, and the inferred intention modulates joint impedance. The experimental comparison covers high fixed impedance, low fixed impedance, and adaptive variable impedance. Across the reported 12 experiments, mean completion times were 19.83 s for high impedance, 15.04 s for low impedance, and 14.58 s for variable impedance. Mean interaction forces were 15.07 N, 11.24 N, and 9.68 N, respectively. Reported trajectory errors were 1.21 mm for high impedance, 1.63 mm for low impedance, and 0.91 mm for variable impedance. The authors report Shapiro–Wilk tests with p greater than 0.05 and paired t-tests indicating significant differences between control modes, although the available reporting does not support reconstruction of every exact p-value, effect size, or pairwise comparison. The paper does not provide a formal stability, passivity, or safety proof. Its open-space framing is experimentally narrowed by use of a fixed reference trajectory, and the evidence does not clearly establish robustness across multiple participants, individual sEMG characteristics, or more complex tasks.
synthesis_role: Primary comparative evidence for intent-conditioned variable impedance in physical human–robot collaboration; useful for the empirical-performance branch of the field map and as a counterpoint to passivity- or stability-certified impedance approaches.
development_link: Connects classical fixed-gain impedance control to human-intent-aware online impedance adaptation. It demonstrates a practical sEMG-based mechanism for changing compliance, while exposing unresolved needs in user-independent intention estimation, formal interaction guarantees, bandwidth-aware transient control, and validation beyond prescribed trajectories.

evidence.locator: Method sections describing sEMG intention estimation and adaptive joint-impedance control
evidence.finding: Surface electromyography signals are used to estimate human motion intention, and the resulting intention estimate drives online adaptation of robot joint impedance.

The paper compares high fixed impedance, low fixed impedance, and adaptive variable impedance and depicts 12 experiments; the full allocation of repetitions and number of distinct participants are not clearly established in the reported material.

evidence.locator: Experimental-results section reporting task completion time
evidence.finding: Mean completion times were 19.83 s under high impedance, 15.04 s under low impedance, and 14.58 s under adaptive variable impedance.
Mean interaction forces were 15.07 N under high impedance, 11.24 N under low impedance, and 9.68 N under adaptive variable impedance.
Reported trajectory errors were 1.21 mm under high impedance, 1.63 mm under low impedance, and 0.91 mm under adaptive variable impedance.

evidence.locator: Statistical-analysis portion of the experimental-results section
evidence.finding: Shapiro–Wilk tests are reported with p greater than 0.05, followed by paired t-tests reported as finding significant differences between control modes; exact p-values and effect sizes are not available for complete independent reconstruction.
No formal proof of closed-loop stability, interaction passivity, collision safety, or bounded human–robot energy exchange is established.
Although framed as an open-space collaboration method, evaluation follows a fixed trajectory, limiting evidence for unrestricted open-space motion.
The authors identify individual variability in sEMG and the need for more general intention-estimation methods and more complex task validation as continuing challenges.

evidence.locator: Experimental traces and discussion of transient response
evidence.finding: Transient interaction-force behavior is associated with sensing/control bandwidth and robot inertia; this indicates a practical boundary on how quickly impedance adaptation can respond.

boundary_conditions: Evaluation uses a prescribed fixed trajectory despite the broader open-space-task framing.
The paper depicts 12 experiments, but the number of distinct human participants and repetition allocation are not sufficiently clear to support population-level inference.
Performance depends on the quality and calibration of user-specific sEMG signals.
Reported results concern the tested robot, sensing pipeline, controller bandwidth, trajectories, and task conditions.
Bandwidth limitations and robot inertia can produce transient interaction-force responses.
The study does not establish performance for contact-rich, collision-prone, highly dynamic, or substantially more complex collaborative tasks.
Reported significance does not substitute for disclosed effect sizes, confidence intervals, or complete pairwise statistical results.
assumptions: Surface electromyography provides a sufficiently timely and informative proxy for the collaborator's motion intention.
The mapping from estimated intention to joint impedance remains appropriate for the tested user and task.
The robot model, trajectory reference, sensing, and low-level control are accurate enough for the adaptive impedance layer to operate as intended.
Comparisons among modes are made under sufficiently similar task and experimental conditions.
The fixed trajectory is an adequate proxy for the open-space collaboration behavior targeted by the method.

reported: Individual differences in sEMG signals limit direct universality of the intention-estimation mechanism.
The experimental task remains tied to a fixed trajectory and does not validate unrestricted open-space collaboration.
Control/sensing bandwidth and robot inertia contribute to transient interaction-force behavior.
Further work is needed on more general learning-based intention estimation and more complex collaborative tasks.
inferred: Because participant count and repeat allocation are unclear, the results cannot support strong cross-user generalization.
Without a formal stability or passivity analysis, improved empirical force and tracking metrics cannot be interpreted as a proof of safe interaction.
Reliance on sEMG calibration may cause degraded or mistimed impedance adaptation under electrode shift, fatigue, signal noise, or users not represented in the evaluation.
The fixed-trajectory protocol may conceal failures arising from abrupt intention changes, unconstrained paths, or conflicting human and robot objectives.

The relatively small difference in mean completion time between variable and low impedance should not be treated as practically decisive without complete uncertainty estimates and pairwise statistics.

verification_status: identity_and_content_bound; quantitative and methodological claims retained as author-reported; participant structure, exact statistical details, stability, safety, and generalization explicitly marked unresolved
